Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Adult male with untreated hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, active smoker, presenting with sudden-onset central chest pressure (7/10) lasting several hours, radiating to left shoulder/arm, with shortness of breath, light-headedness, and nausea. Reports recent exertional dyspnea and calf pain with leg swelling.
- High concern for acute coronary syndrome (ACS) based on classic ischemic features and risk factors (consistent with DDx).
- Pulmonary embolism considered due to dyspnea and reported calf pain/leg swelling (consistent with DDx), though features more typical of ACS.
- Less likely musculoskeletal or gastrointestinal causes (consistent with DDx).
- Immediate action: Emergency ambulance arranged; instructed to remain calm, sip water as needed, avoid taking any medications, inform spouse. Paramedics to assess for cardiac and respiratory causes and transport to hospital.
- Conflict noted: Pediatric assessment template applied to an adult case; many pediatric elements not applicable or not recorded.

Management Plan
- Immediate: Emergency transfer to hospital via ambulance arranged; stay calm; sip water; do not take any medications; wife informed to prepare for hospital visit; paramedics to perform vitals and cardiac monitoring and manage breathing support as needed.
- Hospital focus per discussion: Urgent evaluation for cardiac (heart) and respiratory (lungs) causes of chest symptoms.
- Follow-up: Clinician to book a follow-up appointment after hospital assessment.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Acute Coronary Syndrome (MI/unstable angina) – High likelihood: Exertional central chest pressure with left arm radiation, persistent >2 hours, dyspnea, light-headedness, nausea; risk factors include smoking, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia.
- Pulmonary Embolism – Moderate likelihood: Dyspnea and light-headedness with reported calf pain and leg swelling; less typical chest pain quality, but remains a consideration.
- Musculoskeletal chest wall pain – Low likelihood: Temporal association with activity, but pressure-like central pain with arm radiation and cardiopulmonary symptoms argue against.
